title: Knowledge Worker Productivity Benchmarks: How Your Teams Compare
summary: Productivity benchmarks for knowledge workers: focus time, meeting load and workday span, how to read percentiles, and how to compare your teams.
body_markdown:
**TLDR:** A productivity benchmark shows whether your teams' work patterns are typical for people in similar roles. What to know:


- Benchmark **work patterns** , not output: focus time, meetings and messages, workday span and AI tool use.
- Read benchmarks as **ranges** . The middle half of peers is the normal range; the edges are where to look closer.
- Compare by **role first** . Managers, engineers and sales reps work differently in every industry.
- Start with a **baseline** of your own data, then compare, find the gaps and change one thing at a time.
- Keep it at **team level** . Benchmarks are for fixing how work is organized, not for rating people.


Your engineers say they never get time to think. Your managers go from one meeting to the next all day. Is that normal, or is it a problem only your company has?


A productivity benchmark answers that question by comparing your teams' work patterns with people in similar roles at other organizations. This guide explains what to benchmark for knowledge workers, how to read a benchmark range, why role matters more than industry, and how to run a comparison for your own teams.


## What a productivity benchmark is (and what it is not)


A productivity benchmark is a reference point: how a measure looks across many comparable people or teams. For knowledge workers, the most useful benchmarks describe how the workday is spent, such as hours in meetings or time for focused work, because output is hard to compare across companies.


A benchmark is **not a target** . Sitting at the median for meeting hours only means you are typical, and typical can still be too much. Use a benchmark to spot where your teams differ from peers, then ask why.


It is also **not a score for individuals** . Benchmarks compare groups, and the patterns behind them, such as meeting habits or late-night messages, are set mostly by how teams are organized, not by any one person.


## The metrics to benchmark for knowledge workers


Four groups of measures cover most of what leaders ask about. The definitions below are the ones Worklytics uses in its[data dictionary](https://docs.worklytics.co/knowledge-base/data-dictionary/aggregates-methodology/focus-time-methodology) . Other tools may define the same names differently, so check definitions before you compare numbers from two sources.


### Focus time


Focus time is time in blocks long enough for deep work, with no meetings, email or chat in them. Worklytics counts the average hours per day in blocks of **at least 2 hours** without email, chat or meeting activity, inside working hours. Quiet stretches too short to count are **fragmented time** : the time exists, but it is broken up by interruptions.


Low focus time across a whole team usually comes from meeting schedules or chat habits rather than from the people in it. Roles such as engineers, analysts and writers need it most.


Sample Worklytics report: how meetings and chat break a workday into focus time and fragmented time (sample data).


### Collaboration load: meetings, email and chat


Collaboration load is the time spent in meetings, email and chat. Meeting hours are the most common benchmark question, and two things make them comparable. First, remove calendar entries that are not real meetings, such as focus blocks, reminders and events with one attendee. Second, do not count overlapping time twice. Worklytics' exclusive time method counts each minute once, so time spent in chat during a meeting is not also counted as meeting time.


Look at the mix as well as the total. Large meetings, recurring meetings and 1:1s say different things about how a team works.


### Workday span and after-hours work


Workday span is the time between a person's first and last work activity of the day in digital tools. It is not hours worked, since people take breaks, but a long span day after day is an early sign of strain. After-hours work is activity outside set working hours; Worklytics uses 9:00 to 17:00, Monday to Friday, unless a company sets its own hours. For how these patterns lead to burnout, see[preventing burnout by analyzing collaboration overload](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/preventing-burnout-by-analyzing-collaboration-overload) .


### AI tool use


AI tools now change how much of the work gets done, so many companies benchmark adoption too: the share of people using AI tools and how often they use them. AI adoption has its own benchmarks; see[AI tool adoption rate by industry](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/ai-tool-adoption-rate-by-industry) .


## How to read a benchmark: percentiles and the normal range


Benchmarks are usually shown as percentiles. The **50th percentile** , or median, is the middle value: half of the comparison group is below it and half is above. The **25th and 75th percentiles** mark the edges of the middle half of the group, which is often called the normal range. Worklytics' benchmark gives decile values, every 10th percentile, so you can see the whole spread.


Here is how to read one, with made-up numbers for a single role:


Percentile Focus time per day (made-up example) What it means


25th 1.5 hours A quarter of peers get less focus time


50th (median) 2.5 hours Half of peers get less, half get more


75th 3.5 hours A quarter of peers get more focus time


A team that averages 1.2 hours of focus time a day is below the normal range: most peers in the same role get more uninterrupted time. A team at 2.8 hours is above the median but still inside the normal range, which is typical.


Three habits keep the reading honest:


- **Compare like with like:** the same role, a similar company size and the same metric definition.
- **Know which way is good:** more focus time is usually better, but a longer workday span or more after-hours work is not.
- **Use several weeks of data:** one week with a holiday or a product launch can move a team a long way.


## Why role matters more than industry


A sales rep and a software engineer at the same bank have less in common at work than two engineers at different companies. Managers usually spend more of the day in meetings than the people they manage, because coordinating is much of their job, and sales roles spend more time with customers. So compare by role first, then by company size, and use industry as a last cut.


This is why Worklytics'[Workplace Metrics Benchmark](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/workplace-metrics-benchmark-v2-including-benchmarks-for-sales-software-engineers-line-managers-executives-and-more) splits its data into work profiles, including software engineers, sales professionals, senior leaders, and larger and smaller organizations, alongside line managers and individual contributors.


## How to benchmark your own teams in 4 steps


1. **Measure a baseline.** Collect several weeks of your own data for each metric, using the same definitions as the benchmark. Worklytics' first benchmark report started with 19 of its most widely cited metrics, including workday span, focus time and time spent collaborating.
2. **Split by role and team.** Break results down by role (individual contributor, manager, executive), by function and by team size before you compare, so you compare like with like.
3. **Find the gaps.** Mark where teams fall outside the normal range, and in which direction. Ask the team what is behind a gap before you decide it is a problem.
4. **Change one thing and measure again.** Pick one change, such as a meeting-free morning or shorter default meetings, and compare the same metric a few weeks later. Set targets as a direction or a range, not one exact number.


For the full list of metrics worth tracking, see[employee productivity metrics and KPIs](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/employee-productivity-metrics-kpis) .


## Benchmark without watching individuals


Benchmarking works on group patterns, so it does not need anyone's message content or keystrokes. Choose tools that work from metadata, such as when meetings happen, how many people attend and when messages are sent, that remove or replace personal identifiers, and that only show results for groups above a minimum size. Tell employees what is measured and why. See[how Worklytics handles privacy](https://www.worklytics.co/privacy) .


To see how your teams compare with peers in the same roles,[explore Worklytics benchmarks](https://www.worklytics.co/benchmarks) .


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What are productivity benchmarks?


Productivity benchmarks are reference values for a measure across many comparable people or teams, such as the median hours in meetings per week for managers. They show whether your teams' work patterns are typical, unusually high or unusually low compared with peers in similar roles.


### What are examples of productivity metrics for knowledge workers?


Common ones are focus time (long uninterrupted blocks for deep work), hours in meetings, email and chat volume, workday span (first to last work activity of the day), after-hours work and AI tool use. Pair them with output measures specific to each team, such as tickets closed or deals won.


### What is a good productivity score?


There is no universal score. A benchmark tells you whether a pattern is typical for your role, and each metric has its own good direction: more focus time is usually better, while longer workday spans and more after-hours work are not. Judge each metric against the range for comparable roles rather than one combined number.


### Where do productivity benchmarks come from?


From vendors that collect work data from many organizations. Before you rely on one, ask how large and recent the dataset is, which roles and company sizes it covers, and how each metric is defined. Worklytics builds its benchmark from sanitized, aggregated data from millions of digital work accounts across several hundred thousand people.


### How often should we compare our teams with a benchmark?


Quarterly is enough for most teams. Work patterns change slowly, and comparing every week mostly shows noise from holidays, launches and travel. Check more often only while you are testing a specific change, such as a meeting-free day.
